The syntax is deliberately circular: the heart’s opening is both caused by May’s arrival and offered as proof that May has truly arrived. Nothing else is named—no blossoms, no breeze, no human actor—so the poem reduces the experience of spring to a pure correspondence between world and self.

Formally the haiku is orthodox (5-7-5) yet conspicuously repetitive. Repeating the same five-syllable phrase at beginning and end is a rhetorical device more common in court waka than in Bashō-style haikai; it creates a loop that enacts the very “opening” it describes. This double duty is quietly radical: the poem does not decorate nature; it identifies nature’s arrival with an alteration in consciousness. The circular structure also undercuts any linear narrative of cause and effect; instead, inner and outer change are presented as mutually confirming aspects of a single event.  

Stylistically, the diction is plain, almost childlike in its simplicity, yet the conceptual compression is sophisticated. By refusing further imagery the poet forces the reader to experience the “opening” as an abstract event rather than a pictorial one—an austere move that aligns the poem with the minimalist strain of modern haiku while still honoring the classical expectation that a seasonal word carry affective weight. The result is a small, self-verifying loop in which language, season, and feeling coincide.
